options.text: Your playlist will keep guessing what you like; this weekend, pledge to the one station that knows where you live.
options.why: Calls readers to pledge and echoes the like/live contrast from sentence 4.

options.text: Radio has changed a great deal in forty years, and it will surely keep changing in the decades ahead.
options.why: Generic reflection on radio; no call to donate and no link to sentence 4.

options.text: Streaming apps offer millions of songs, so perhaps local radio like 89.7 has simply had its day and should quietly sign off.
options.why: Undercuts the column's argument by suggesting the station should close instead of urging support.

options.text: Hal Pruitt's nineteen hours on the air during the flood deserve a bronze plaque in the station's front lobby.
options.why: Focuses on one volunteer rather than urging donations or returning to the streaming contrast.

options.text: Some people in Harrow Bend prefer podcasts to the radio on most ordinary weeknights after dinner.
options.why: Shifts to listening habits generally, not the flood-night audience.

options.text: Judging by the calls the station logged, hundreds of households in Harrow Bend were listening that night.
options.why: Replaces the absolute claim with a qualified, evidence-based estimate that still shows wide reach.

options.text: Absolutely everyone in Harrow Bend, without a single exception, had the station on all through that night.
options.why: Intensifies the overstatement rather than qualifying it.

options.text: A few people in Harrow Bend may have had their radios turned on that night.
options.why: Qualifies the claim but abandons the sense of wide reach the writer wants.

options.text: Algorithms are useless, and anyone who relies on them is foolishly ignoring what really matters in life and in this town.
options.why: Remains absolute and adds a dismissive jab; acknowledges nothing.

options.text: An algorithm may be good at finding me a new song, but no algorithm found my neighbor a dry cot.
options.why: Concedes a real strength of streaming, then reasserts the station's local value using the flood detail.

options.text: Many streaming companies were founded in the past two decades by large technology firms based in distant coastal cities.
options.why: Offers off-topic background instead of a concession tied to local service.

options.text: Algorithms are better than radio in nearly every way, including during floods, storms, and other local emergencies like the one in March.
options.why: Concedes so much it contradicts the paragraph's point, even about the March flood.

options.text: Ordinary people are truly the backbone of the station, and without their steady help it simply could not survive.
options.why: Restates the claim without any specific example.

options.text: Many community stations across the country face similar money troubles in the streaming era, from Maine to rural Oregon.
options.why: Generalizes nationally; gives no example of local people keeping this station alive.

options.text: Last winter, when the roof leaked, a local roofer patched it for free and the bakery next door paid for shingles.
options.why: Concrete example of ordinary residents sustaining the station.

options.text: The transmitter that needs replacing was installed when the station first went on the air forty years ago this spring.
options.why: Repeats the transmitter detail and does not show people sustaining the station.

options.text: The station's budget is a total disaster, and honestly it's a miracle the thing hasn't collapsed already.
options.why: Still flippant and disparaging, discouraging donors.

options.text: The station runs on a budget smaller than the high school band's, which makes its survival close to remarkable.
options.why: Respectful and admiring; sets up 'Yet it does survive' and keeps the local detail.

options.text: The station is very well funded by state grants and has never had much trouble paying its bills on time.
options.why: Contradicts the need for the pledge drive, invents funding, and makes sentence 12 illogical.

options.text: Fiscal resources allocated to the station remain suboptimal relative to its operational requirements and projected capital expenditure needs.
options.why: Stiff bureaucratic jargon, not sincere or warm for newspaper readers.

options.text: midnight Sunday, because a donation
options.why: Grammatical, but falsely claims the schedule exists because of the donation rate.

options.text: midnight Sunday a donation
options.why: Creates a run-on sentence with no punctuation between clauses.

options.text: midnight Sunday, and, a donation
options.why: The comma after 'and' is incorrect and interrupts the clause.

options.text: midnight Sunday; a donation
options.why: A semicolon correctly joins two independent clauses, fixing the comma splice.

options.text: Honestly, anyone who skips this concert is missing out, and frankly they should be embarrassed to admit they had better things to do that night.
options.why: Scolding tone suits neither the audience nor the column, and it omits cooperation.

options.text: Hear it yourself on May 10 at the Grange Hall, and listen for the oboe: it rises only because forty others chose to play softer.
options.why: Invites readers to the concert and recalls the rehearsal moment that shows cooperation.

options.text: The concert is on May 10 at the Grange Hall, tickets cost eight dollars at the door, and there will be lemonade and cookies during intermission.
options.why: Gives concert details but drops the cooperation point entirely.

options.text: In the end, cooperation is what holds an orchestra together, just as it holds together a family, a team, or any other group of people.
options.why: Restates the theme but never urges readers to attend the concert.

options.text: The orchestra has rehearsed in the Fenwick Grange Hall since 1987 and gives two free concerts there every spring and fall.
options.why: A statement of fact that needs no proof and previews nothing.

options.text: I came to believe the orchestra's players listen carefully to one another, section by section, before any of them plays a note.
options.why: Covers the rehearsal but does not preview the comparison to the town council.

options.text: Watching them, I came to believe an orchestra works because its players listen before they play, a habit our leaders could borrow.
options.why: Arguable claim about listening that previews both the rehearsal and the council comparison.

options.text: Music has brought people together in every culture and every century throughout human history, from ancient temples to modern stadiums.
options.why: Sweeping claim far beyond the column's local focus; no preview of the council point.

options.text: Some musicians in this orchestra have played together for decades, carpool to rehearsals, and know one another's families, jobs, and hometowns well.
options.why: Shifts to a different topic and drops both the concession and the cooperation claim.

options.text: Most musicians care only about their own parts, and the group sound that results is mostly an accident nobody really plans for.
options.why: Contradicts the column's argument rather than qualifying it.

options.text: Players still want their own parts to sound good, of course, but the best of them will step back when the music needs it.
options.why: Concedes individual pride and still affirms cooperation, removing the absolute claim.

options.text: Every single musician in every orchestra in the world cares far more about the group than about anything else, including their own playing.
options.why: Intensifies the overstatement instead of qualifying it.

options.text: The oboist, a dental hygienist named Ruth Palko, has played with the group for nine years and teaches lessons on weekends.
options.why: Adds a detail but no commentary connecting the evidence to the claim.

options.text: This proves that the oboe is the most important instrument in any orchestra and that composers should always give it the melody.
options.why: Draws a conclusion the evidence does not support and misses the cooperation point.

options.text: After that, the orchestra moved on to rehearse a lively march, full of brass fanfares, that would close the spring concert.
options.why: Continues the narration rather than explaining the moment's significance.

options.text: The fix came not from one player trying harder but from everyone agreeing to make room for a single voice.
options.why: Explains that the improvement resulted from the group yielding, linking the evidence to cooperation.

options.text: signaling that she has largely abandoned her claim to authorship, so that readers who revere the original novelist will not feel threatened by the rest of the post
options.why: She concedes only story and characters and immediately rebuts with the carpenter analogy; she does not abandon the authorship claim.

options.text: suggesting that readers who hold the objection are in reasonable company, so that her rebuttal reads as a conclusion she reached rather than a defense of her own interests
options.why: By owning the objection and granting 'There is something to this,' she disarms readers who share it and makes the carpenter rebuttal seem considered rather than self-serving.

options.text: showing that the objection is trivial enough to be raised casually over dinner, so that readers will dismiss outright the view that the story belongs to the novelist
options.why: She treats the objection seriously ('There is something to this,' 'I would not want credit for her'); the dinner-party detail shows familiarity, not triviality.

options.text: establishing that her audience consists chiefly of literary insiders who attend such gatherings, so that the argument can rely on their specialized knowledge of publishing customs and the conventions of prize juries
options.why: Nothing in the passage limits the audience to insiders; the final paragraph addresses prize runners, reviewers and ordinary readers.

options.text: evidence that the prize's judgment of most of its shortlist depended on translators' work, which makes the omission of their names consequential rather than clerical
options.why: The detail shows the jury could only read those four books through translation, sharpening the point that the press release omitted the people responsible for what the jury read.

options.text: a concession that the prize rightly focused on authors, since the jury could only assess the stories rather than the prose of most entries
options.why: The sentence intensifies the criticism of the press release; it does not grant that the focus on authors was correct.

options.text: a claim that the jury lacked the linguistic qualifications to evaluate foreign novels fairly, which the rest of the paragraph proceeds to support
options.why: The writer never argues the jury was unqualified; the sentence is a factual detail supporting the omission point, not a thesis about the jury's competence.

options.text: evidence that translated novels now outnumber English-language novels on literary shortlists across the industry, a trend which explains the writer's interest in this particular prize
options.why: One shortlist with four of six translated books is not offered as a trend across shortlists; the passage makes no such generalization.

options.text: Publishers fear that a second name on the cover will mark a book as foreign and therefore difficult for buyers in the sales meeting
options.why: That claim concerns marketing in paragraph 5; the weather example is about linguistic choice, not sales fears.

options.text: A sentence is a set of choices that a second language cannot reproduce but can only answer, and the translator's answer is taken as the author's
options.why: The verb with a double meaning has no English equivalent, forcing the translator to choose, and 'the English reader would believe the author had chosen it' directly illustrates the claim in the preceding sentence.

options.text: Translators have cultivated a monkish modesty that treats visibility as a form of vanity and keeps their names off covers and out of press releases
options.why: The modesty claim appears in paragraph 5 as a cause of invisibility; the example does not touch translators' attitudes toward credit.

options.text: The story, the characters, and the architecture of a novel belong to the original novelist rather than to the person who translates it
options.why: The example does involve Aalvik's heroine, but it is used to show the translator's authorship of the sentence, not the novelist's ownership of story.

options.text: Enumeration of three causes that together form a self-reinforcing loop, used to show that invisibility is a maintained convention rather than a natural fact
options.why: The question in the first sentence is answered by three 'partly because' causes and then the colon sentence shows the causes feeding one another, which supports the claim that the convention persists by choice and habit.

options.text: Classification of translators into types according to how much modesty they display, used to show which translators deserve to be named on covers
options.why: Translators are not sorted into types; modesty is mentioned once as a cause, and the writer argues all translators should be named.

options.text: Comparison and contrast between publishers and reviewers, used to show that the two groups have opposite reasons for ignoring translators and therefore require opposite remedies
options.why: The three groups are presented as contributing to one shared effect, not as contrasting opposites, and no separate remedies are distinguished.

options.text: Narration of the writer's own experiences with publishers, used to show that she has personally suffered from each of the practices described
options.why: The paragraph offers general causes, not narrated episodes; the only personal note is 'I confess,' which admits a shared habit.

options.text: separates the three causes listed earlier from the writer's confession, so that readers see her own modesty as the decisive reason translators go unnamed
options.why: The confession occurs in the previous sentence; the colon introduces the summary effect, and the three causes are given equal weight.

options.text: announces that an explanation of the word 'circular' follows, and the two clauses after it then trace the loop the word names, so form and claim match
options.why: The colon sets up the explanation, and the paired 'because...because' clauses move from unnamed to unimportant and back to unnamed, enacting the circle.

options.text: introduces a list of further parties who contribute to the convention, so that the explanation extends beyond the three groups named in the paragraph
options.why: No additional parties follow the colon; what follows is a two-step causal loop about translators being unnamed and seeming unimportant.

options.text: creates a pause that softens the accusation against publishers and reviewers, so that the tone of the paragraph becomes more conciliatory before the proposal
options.why: The sentence does not soften anything; it states the self-reinforcing problem bluntly, and the shift to proposal comes in the next paragraph.

options.text: The wall made sense when it was built, but its effect on the beach in front of it deserves a closer look.
options.why: Respects the reasoning of wall supporters and then turns toward the evidence in sentence 8.

options.text: Some people like walls and some people like dunes, and everyone is entitled to an opinion about how the town should handle its coast.
options.why: Vague and does not point to the drawback the writer wants to raise.

options.text: Supporters of the wall were frankly shortsighted, though they probably meant well when they voted to pour concrete below Pell Street.
options.why: Still insults the audience, which undercuts the goal of respect.

options.text: The wall has been a complete success, and nobody could reasonably question its value to the town or the families living behind it.
options.why: Drops the drawback and contradicts sentence 8.

options.text: Beach grass is a hardy plant that can grow in salty, sandy soil where few other plants manage to survive.
options.why: Describes the plant but offers no evidence that dunes protect the coast.

options.text: At the town's older restored dune near Hollis Beach, our stakes showed almost no bluff loss over three years of storms.
options.why: Gives measured evidence linking dunes directly to reduced erosion.

options.text: Erosion is a problem that affects shorelines on every continent and costs governments large sums each year in repairs to roads and harbors.
options.why: Addresses erosion generally, not the effectiveness of dunes.

options.text: Several residents we interviewed said they find the dunes at Little Cove prettier than the gray concrete of the Pell Street wall.
options.why: Shows preference about appearance, not proof of protection.

options.text: What we found, and what we discovered, was that the bluff edge moved about two feet a year since 1990.
options.why: Keeps the redundancy and garbles the verb tense.

options.text: In the end, we discovered the edge of the bluff retreats every single year by a yearly average of two feet.
options.why: Swaps words but stays redundant ('every single year', 'yearly') and drops the date.

options.text: We found that the bluff edge has retreated quite a bit over the years since the early nineties.
options.why: Concise but loses the precise figure and date.

options.text: We found that the bluff edge has retreated an average of about two feet a year since 1990.
options.why: Removes the repeated 'found out and discovered' and 'every single' while keeping all facts.

options.text: Because rebuilding costs more after a storm, moving buildings is expensive.
options.why: Turns the relationship around into a false cause.

options.text: Moving buildings is expensive, but rebuilding them after a storm costs more.
options.why: Uses 'but' to show contrast and keeps the comparison clear and concise.

options.text: Moving buildings is expensive, so rebuilding them after a storm costs more.
options.why: 'So' wrongly implies the moving cost causes the rebuilding cost.

options.text: Moving buildings is expensive, rebuilding them after a storm costs more.
options.why: Comma splice, with no word showing the contrast.

options.text: Referees in the league must complete an eight-hour certification course before they can officiate any game, including scrimmages for the youngest players.
options.why: About referee training but offers no evidence linking fans to quitting.

options.text: In the league's exit survey, 17 of the 23 departing referees listed verbal abuse from spectators as their main reason for leaving.
options.why: Directly links the quitting to fan treatment with specific evidence.

options.text: Everyone knows that fans at youth games are louder and ruder now than at any time in history, especially at weekend tournaments with big crowds.
options.why: A sweeping assertion, not evidence, and it does not tie the behavior to quitting.

options.text: The league pays its teen referees 25 dollars per game, which is a little more than many part-time jobs pay.
options.why: About pay, not about fan behavior causing departures.

options.text: This shortage matters because
options.why: Shows that sentence 6 explains the consequence of the loss.

options.text: Despite this referee shortage,
options.why: Suggests canceled games happen in spite of the shortage, reversing the cause.

options.text: In a similar way,
options.why: Sentence 6 is not a parallel example; it is a consequence.

options.text: In contrast to this,
options.why: Sentence 6 does not contrast with the loss; it follows from it.

options.text: Specifically,
options.why: Treats sentence 14 as an illustration or detail of the opposing view.

options.text: Additionally,
options.why: Signals agreement or addition rather than contrast.

options.text: However,
options.why: Signals that sentence 14 challenges the view in sentence 13.

options.text: Therefore,
options.why: Presents sentence 14 as a result of 13, which it is not.

options.text: resentment toward county council members who were prepared to close the libraries
options.why: The passage reports the council's reliance on the chart neutrally; it blames the chart's design and the lack of trained readers, not the council's motives.

options.text: interest in limiting what the district spends on new curricular materials each school year
options.why: Cost appears only as a preview detail (38 dollars per student) and is never connected to the surveyor; the anecdote does not address budget concerns.

options.text: conviction that only trained specialists can be relied on to interpret data correctly
options.why: The writer stresses the opposite: 'He was not an expert; he simply knew which question to ask,' arguing the skill is teachable to ordinary students.

options.text: belief that public decisions should depend on informed scrutiny rather than on chance
options.why: The surveyor's question saved the libraries, and the writer frames this as luck ('the luck of who happens to be in the room') that the district can replace with deliberate teaching so that 'a few hundred more people' are there next time.

options.text: students rarely notice chart manipulation on their own, but even brief instruction measurably improves their attention to it
options.why: The figures (fewer than one in five noticed the axis; just over half after five minutes) directly back 'The need is not speculative' and 'Five minutes moved the needle.'

options.text: the proposed unit should be housed in the civics or English sequence rather than offered as a separate course
options.why: Placement of the unit is the writer's response to the time objection in paragraph 4; the diagnostic data say nothing about where the unit belongs.

options.text: mathematics classes already give students most of the skills needed to evaluate charts built by other people
options.why: Paragraph 4 argues the reverse, that almost no class teaches students to judge others' charts; the diagnostic shows the skill is largely absent.

options.text: a visual argument can mislead a viewer more quickly than a written argument and leaves no false sentence behind
options.why: This is the claim of paragraph 5 about charts in civic life; the diagnostic measures student perception, not the speed of deception relative to prose.

options.text: conceding that the fields overlap but insisting that some curricular redundancy is harmless
options.why: The writer calls the overlap concern 'mistaken' and never argues that redundancy is acceptable; the rebuttal denies the overlap rather than tolerating it.

options.text: granting the concern as fair and shrinking the proposal to a four-week unit
options.why: This describes the writer's handling of the time objection; the overlap objection is rejected, not granted.

options.text: distinguishing between producing charts correctly and evaluating charts that others have produced
options.why: The writer says mathematics teaches students 'to build charts correctly' while 'almost no class' teaches what to do when someone else has built one, then crystallizes the distinction with the cooking analogy.

options.text: proposing that the unit be absorbed into existing mathematics courses to avoid duplication
options.why: The writer places the unit inside civics or English, not mathematics, and does so in response to the time concern, not the overlap concern.

options.text: Paragraph 2 defines the skill and states the recommendation; paragraph 3 offers evidence that the skill is lacking and can be taught
options.why: Paragraph 2 defines chart literacy and recommends a required unit; paragraph 3 opens 'The need is not speculative' and supplies diagnostic results showing both the deficit and the gain from instruction.

options.text: Paragraph 2 raises a theoretical distinction that paragraph 3 challenges with results from the district's own students, who already read charts skeptically
options.why: The diagnostic supports the writer's position rather than challenging it; most students missed the truncated axis, so paragraph 3 confirms, not contests, the need described in paragraph 2.

options.text: Paragraph 2 proposes a definition that paragraph 3 then narrows by showing which parts of it students already possess without any formal instruction
options.why: Paragraph 3 does not revise the definition; it shows students mostly lack the skill, with fewer than one in five noticing the axis.

options.text: Paragraph 2 states the recommendation in general terms; paragraph 3 restates it with more specific scheduling details and a proposed budget
options.why: Scheduling details (a four-week unit inside civics or English) appear in paragraph 4 and cost in paragraph 6; paragraph 3 presents data rather than restating the proposal.

options.text: The season was long and demanding, and members gave up many Saturdays and several holiday breaks to keep working on Marmalade.
options.why: Offers evidence of effort and commitment, not of what members learned, so it supports a different claim.

options.text: Research consistently shows that hands-on clubs like robotics teach students more than classroom lectures do, which is why nearly every school funds them.
options.why: Makes a generic, unsourced claim about clubs and schools in general and says nothing about these particular members.

options.text: Learning a great deal is the main reason any club deserves the school's financial support, which the board should remember.
options.why: Functions as commentary about why learning matters rather than as evidence that learning occurred.

options.text: Two members who could not define a gear ratio in September wrote the technical notebook that the judges scored in April.
options.why: Gives a concrete before-and-after example of skill growth in named terms that directly supports the claim about learning.

options.text: A mismatched wheel pair is a common error in beginner builds, according to the instruction booklet that came with the kit.
options.why: Explains the error rather than comparing the approach, and shifts attention to the mistake instead of the problem-solving.

options.text: Like a team that forfeits rather than finishes, we knew from the start that quitting was always an option for us.
options.why: The comparison contradicts sentence 7, which shows the team persisting, and undercuts the argument about efficient problem-solving.

options.text: Like a mechanic who checks the tires before rebuilding the engine, we had learned to look for the simplest explanation first.
options.why: Offers a familiar analogy that clarifies the method in sentence 7 and frames it as a learned, efficient habit.

options.text: Robots, like people, have good days and bad days, and November was simply a bad month for Marmalade and its builders.
options.why: Has the form of a comparison but says nothing about how the team diagnosed or fixed the problem.

options.text: The adjudicating personnel expressed considerable astonishment regarding the operational status of our apparatus, a sentiment they conveyed with notable effusiveness upon its arrival.
options.why: Swings to inflated, stilted diction that sounds pompous and does not match the plain voice of the rest of the report.

options.text: Two of the judges told our adviser that they had not expected a first-year team to arrive with a fully functioning robot.
options.why: Uses measured, specific wording suited to a formal report and attributes the reaction to particular judges without exaggeration.

options.text: Honestly, the judges were pretty shocked that a rookie team like ours even pulled off a working bot at its first competition.
options.why: Retains the casual, conversational register of the original, including slang like 'pulled off' and 'bot.'

options.text: Every judge at the competition agreed that Marmalade was the most impressive robot of the day, and several asked to photograph it.
options.why: Replaces the casual tone with sweeping claims the writer cannot support, especially given the ninth-place finish in sentence 2.

options.text: Several of the students who joined had never used a power drill before, however, by March they were teaching the eighth graders who visited on shadow day.
options.why: A conjunctive adverb set off by commas cannot join two independent clauses; the comma splice remains.

options.text: Several of the students who joined had never used a power drill before by March, they were teaching the eighth graders who visited on shadow day.
options.why: Moves 'by March' to the first clause, changing the meaning, and still leaves a comma splice.

options.text: Several of the students who joined had never used a power drill before; by March they were teaching the eighth graders who visited on shadow day.
options.why: A semicolon correctly joins two closely related independent clauses and keeps 'by March' attached to the teaching.

options.text: Several of the students who joined had never used a power drill before, by March, they were teaching the eighth graders, who visited on shadow day.
options.why: Adds commas but never supplies a semicolon or coordinating conjunction, so the two clauses are still spliced.

options.text: A newspaper campaign that has stirred public alarm about bees by exaggerating a single incident of a child being stung several times while poking a backyard hive
options.why: The Evening Courier headline and the stung boy belong to the 1923 narrative in paragraph 3, not to the present occasion that prompted the essay.

options.text: A proposal before the council to repeal a long-standing ordinance that has kept hives out of the city limits since the early twentieth century, a ban the writer hopes to see lifted
options.why: The ban was already repealed in 1981 (paragraph 5); the present debate concerns permitting a specific resident's hives, not lifting an existing ban.

options.text: A council debate over a resident's request to keep hives, during which a speaker voiced an assumption about the city's past that the writer believes the archive disproves
options.why: Paragraph 1 describes the hearing on Priya Castellanos's hives and the councilman's remark that bees 'do not belong in a modern city'; the writer's archival evidence throughout answers that remark, and paragraph 6 returns to it directly.

options.text: The recent discovery in the municipal archive of a ledger that overturns what historians had previously assumed about the city's earliest beekeepers and the trades they practiced
options.why: The ledger is described as surviving in the archive, but nothing suggests it was newly discovered or that it overturned any prior scholarly assumption.

options.text: Paragraph 4 withdraws the interpretation of paragraph 3 by admitting that the injury to the boy made the ordinance a reasonable and even necessary precaution for a crowded city
options.why: The writer concedes the injury was real but explicitly argues the harm was not large enough to justify erasing the practice; the ordinance is not called reasonable or necessary.

options.text: Paragraph 4 supplies the archival evidence, drawn from council minutes and the boy's medical records, that the interpretation offered in paragraph 3 had asserted without documentation
options.why: Paragraph 4 cites no council minutes or medical records; it reasons about proportion, and the documentation (headline, ordinance, household count) is already in paragraph 3.

options.text: Paragraph 4 moves the narrative forward to a later decade in order to show the long-term consequences of the ordinance described in paragraph 3
options.why: Paragraph 4 stays with the 1923 episode and reasons about it; the move to later decades happens in paragraph 5.

options.text: Paragraph 4 acknowledges a legitimate objection to the interpretation in paragraph 3 and then reframes the issue from whether harm is possible to whether it is proportionate
options.why: Paragraph 4 opens by refusing to 'pretend the worries were all invented,' grants the sting and the mother's anger, then uses the repeated 'The question was' sentences to shift the issue to the size of the harm relative to what was lost.

options.text: set the modest requirements of bees against the larger return they provide, framing the exchange as plainly favorable to the city
options.why: The matched openings invite direct comparison; the first sentence's colon lists only a roof, a water dish and patience, while the second expands into a reminder that the city is a living thing, making the trade appear obviously worthwhile.

options.text: present a list of hazards associated with hives before conceding that those hazards are outweighed by the honey they produce
options.why: The colon in the first sentence introduces simple needs, not hazards, and the return described is a reminder about the city's nature, not honey.

options.text: suggest that the demands bees make and the benefits they provide are roughly equal, so the city's choice is a matter of taste
options.why: The first sentence names a 'small' request and the second a much larger return; the balance of the structure highlights an imbalance in favor of keeping bees, not an even trade.

options.text: convey the writer's uncertainty about whether the benefits of beekeeping, however appealing in principle, can ever be measured against its costs
options.why: The paragraph is assertive throughout; the parallel sentences and the short closing line express confidence, not doubt.

options.text: signals that she has listened to their earlier objections, which earns a hearing from skeptics before she begins to rebut them
options.why: She voices the objection in the audience's own terms, calls it fair, and promises to take it seriously; acknowledging prior forum discussion shows respect for the listeners' views before the rebuttal in the following sentences.

options.text: implies that the council has ignored the riders for years, which shames the officials present into reconsidering the proposal
options.why: The speaker's manner toward the objection is respectful ('a fair objection'); nothing in paragraph 3 shames officials or accuses them of years of neglect.

options.text: reminds listeners that the trial data were presented at an earlier meeting, so they should already accept her conclusion
options.why: The passage never says the trial data were presented earlier; what was heard before is the objection, not the evidence.

options.text: suggests that the objection is tiresome and repetitive, which allows her to dismiss it quickly without offering any new evidence or argument
options.why: She explicitly refuses to 'wave it away' and immediately supplies new trial statistics, the opposite of dismissal.

options.text: invokes a city service the listeners already accept without a headcount, so plowing the path looks like consistency rather than a special favor
options.why: Sentence 19 points out that the town never asks whether enough people walk on Fenwick Avenue to justify shoveling; the analogy transfers that accepted value to the path, answering the headcount objection of paragraph 3.

options.text: shows that pedestrians are also undercounted in winter, so the town should install new counters on Fenwick Avenue before plowing any more paths
options.why: The sidewalk is a point of comparison, not a second problem; the passage proposes nothing about counting pedestrians or delaying plowing.

options.text: stirs sympathy for the ninth-grader whose parents leave early, so listeners feel guilty about any objection to the plowing cost
options.why: The ninth-grader does add emotional weight, but the comparison itself works through the audience's existing assumption about sidewalks, not through guilt about one child.

options.text: proves that bicycle paths are cheaper to clear than sidewalks, so the budget argument in the next paragraph becomes unnecessary
options.why: No cost comparison between paths and sidewalks appears anywhere; the budget figures come later and are presented as necessary, not superfluous.

options.text: It restates the opening anecdote in budgetary terms so that the audience sees the January morning as a cost to the clinic
options.why: Paragraph 5 does not return to the anecdote or the clinic; the opening image is revisited in paragraph 6, not here.

options.text: It expands the argument beyond plowing to the broader question of how the town funds its entire snow budget each winter
options.why: The budget total appears only to make the eleven-thousand-dollar figure look small; the paragraph narrows rather than expands the request.

options.text: It narrows the request to a modest, costed proposal with stated limits, heading off the charge of overpromising before the closing appeal
options.why: Sentences 23-26 admit that some mornings will remain impossible, then specify a precise schedule and dollar figure, moving from the principle of paragraph 4 to a concrete ask before the image of paragraph 6.

options.text: It withdraws the demand made in paragraph 4 by admitting that the path cannot be made safe on every winter morning
options.why: The admission about four or five bad mornings is real, but it qualifies the request rather than withdrawing it; the same paragraph states the demand explicitly.

options.text: use the occasion of a bus route's final run to argue that transit should be valued as a civic institution rather than by its fare revenue
options.why: The obituary frame (sentences 1-6), the central claim that a bus is a public room (10), the rebuttal of the fare statistic (13-15), and the definition of an institution (24) all serve this purpose.

options.text: evaluate whether on-demand shuttles can realistically cover the same territory as a fixed route serving four thousand riders, concluding that telephone dispatch will leave the cannery district underserved
options.why: The shuttles come up only in paragraph 4 as a concession, and the writer explicitly holds off judging how they perform (18), so she draws no such conclusion.

options.text: persuade the city council to reverse its decision and restore the Number 6 route before the on-demand shuttles begin operating and its four thousand riders scatter
options.why: The writer never calls for restoration; she treats the line as gone (31) and even promises to praise the shuttles if they succeed (18).

options.text: record the sentimental details of a last ride, from the folding chair to the applause, so that longtime passengers will have a keepsake of the route they loved and lost
options.why: The narrative details in paragraphs 5 and 6 serve the argument about institutions and civic obligation, not a commemorative keepsake; the essay repeatedly turns to policy and value.

options.text: "A transit line is not a pipe for moving bodies from one point to another; it is a public room on wheels, and a room is judged by who can get into it."
options.why: Sentence 10 states the governing idea that every later paragraph develops: the riders the number cannot see (14), unconditional service (20), and the final question of who the city is for (31).

options.text: "They found that the Six recovered only 23 percent of its operating cost from fares, compared with 41 percent on the express routes that run from the suburbs to the financial district."
options.why: Sentence 12 reports the consultants' evidence, which the writer concedes and then argues against; it is the counterargument's data, not her claim.

options.text: "Some of the Six's riders will be served well enough by the on-demand shuttles, which can be summoned by telephone and which, on paper, cover the same territory."
options.why: Sentence 17 is a remark about a single alternative service, not the overarching argument about what a transit line is.

options.text: "I will concede that nostalgia makes a poor transportation policy. If the shuttles turn out to be prompt and cheap, I will say so in this column."
options.why: Sentences 16 and 18 are a concession and a qualification that limit the writer's position so she can rebut it; they do not express the thesis.

options.text: announcing that the essay will compare the Number 6 to the ride-hailing sedans that now carry its former passengers, weighing their speed against its reliability
options.why: Ride-hailing sedans appear once in the survivors list (3) and are never developed; the comparison in paragraph 4 is with shuttles and is only one part of the argument.

options.text: presenting a chronological history of the route that the later paragraphs will fill in with dates and personnel from 1963 to the final run
options.why: Apart from the age of the route, the passage offers no chronology; later paragraphs are organized by claim and evidence, not by time.

options.text: casting the budget as a fatal illness and the riders as survivors, so that the financial rationale is already framed as a loss to be contested
options.why: Sentences 1 and 3 apply obituary conventions ironically; the 'illness called a budget' sets up the rebuttal of the fare statistic in paragraph 3, and the stranded survivors anticipate the question of who the city is for (31).

options.text: establishing that the writer is a neutral observer who will weigh the consultants' figures against passenger sentiment without taking a side on the route's fate
options.why: The wry obituary framing and the detail of the dispatcher's folding chair signal sympathy for the route from the start; the writer openly takes a side in paragraphs 2 through 6.

options.text: It grants the accuracy of a statistic and then offers specific riders as examples of value the statistic cannot capture
options.why: Sentences 11-13 present and concede the figure; sentence 14 enumerates three concrete riders; sentence 15 draws the general point that fares are not what a bus produces.

options.text: It traces a cause-and-effect chain showing how the route's low fare recovery led inevitably to its cancellation by the council
options.why: The paragraph does not explain the cancellation decision; it accepts the number (13) and then argues about what the number omits (14-15).

options.text: It narrates the writer's own ride along the route to show readers the neighborhoods the consultants failed to visit
options.why: The ride narration occurs in paragraphs 1, 5, and 6; paragraph 3 is built on the consultants' report and representative riders, not on the writer's trip.

options.text: It compares express routes with the crosstown route in order to argue that the suburban express routes should have been cut instead
options.why: The express figure appears only inside the consultants' finding (12); the writer never proposes cutting express routes and instead disputes fare recovery as a measure.

options.text: introduces a direct quotation from the consultants' report that the writer then proceeds to challenge, letting their own words about the riders expose the weakness of their method
options.why: Nothing after the colon is quoted; the material is the writer's own catalogue of riders, and the consultants' finding was already paraphrased in sentence 12.

options.text: creates a hesitant pause that signals the writer's uncertainty about whether the riders truly outweigh the fare figures she has just admitted are accurate
options.why: The surrounding sentences (13, 15) are assertive; the colon announces a confident reveal, not hesitation.

options.text: turns an abstract assertion about the limits of a statistic into a concrete roster of people, so the reveal carries the weight of evidence
options.why: Before the colon is a general claim ('what the number cannot see'); after it come three specific riders (14), which make the abstraction tangible and set up the generalization in 15.

options.text: joins two independent claims of equal importance so that readers weigh the statistic and the riders as competing facts, leaving the final judgment to them
options.why: The colon does not balance two equal claims; it subordinates the list to the opening assertion, which the list illustrates.

content.text:
I lengthened 8 wrong options across Questions 1, 3, 4 and 5. Questions 2 and 6 are unchanged.

- **Lengths now:** in every question, each wrong option is about 85–115% of the key's word count. Question 6's wordy option (30 words) is the one exception, explained below.
- **Options longer than the key:** in two questions (1 and 5), one wrong option is now longer than the key. In Question 6 the original wordy option is also longer than the key.
- **Flaws kept:** none of the additions make a wrong option more defensible. The tone in Question 1 stays casual, the generalization in Question 5 gets broader, and the added Andromeda fact in Question 4 is still beside the point.
- **Question 6 exception:** option 3 is 30 words against a 23-word key. I left it because being wordy is its flaw, and it's already longer than the key. That still leaves a smaller length cue on the key, since the key is the second-longest option.

options.text: Honestly, those Cutler Avenue globes are a total eyesore, and you folks should rip every one of them out tomorrow, no matter what anyone else says.
options.why: Too casual and combative for council testimony, and it ignores the earlier image.

options.text: Astronomy has given me decades of joy, and I hope that more residents of Larkhaven will join our club on Saturdays and discover it for themselves.
options.why: Promotes the club rather than requesting any action on the ordinance.

options.text: Thank you for your time this evening, and I would be happy to answer any questions the council may have for me about my remarks.
options.why: Appropriately formal, but makes no request and recalls nothing from the testimony.

options.text: I urge you to require shielded fixtures in Ordinance 14-B, so that the next child at our eyepiece sees a galaxy instead of a haze.
options.why: Formal, makes a specific request about the ordinance, and echoes the girl's gray haze from sentence 7.

options.text: Quarry Hill Road is a quiet street, and in summer my neighbors often sit outside on their porches after dinner.
options.why: Adds neighborhood detail but never mentions the ordinance or why she is testifying.

options.text: I am here as a member of the Larkhaven Stargazers Club to speak on Ordinance 14-B, the streetlight replacement plan.
options.why: Names her role and the specific agenda item, so the introduction leads into the testimony.

options.text: Before I retired, I worked as a pharmacist at a small drugstore on the east side of town for many years.
options.why: Gives personal background that has nothing to do with lighting or the agenda item.

options.text: Many cities around the world are now debating how much artificial light their residents actually need at night.
options.why: Talks about a global debate instead of the specific local agenda item.

options.text: Light pollution has become a growing problem facing many towns and cities across the country and around the world in recent decades.
options.why: A general observation that previews none of the draft's specific argument.

options.text: Tonight I want to share my lifelong love of astronomy, a hobby I have enjoyed ever since I was a child.
options.why: Personal and not arguable; it previews neither the lighting problem nor the solution.

options.text: I will ask the council to ban all outdoor lighting in Larkhaven after midnight in order to protect the sky.
options.why: Proposes a ban that the draft never argues for; the draft calls for shielding, not darkness.

options.text: I will argue that unshielded streetlights are erasing our night sky and that shielded fixtures could restore it at no added cost.
options.why: Takes an arguable position and previews both the problem (paragraph 2) and the solution (paragraph 3).

options.text: The telescope was working fine; what she saw was the glow of Cutler Avenue covering a sky our children once shared.
options.why: Turns the anecdote into evidence by blaming the haze on the streetlights, which supports the claim.

options.text: Telescopes like mine can cost several hundred dollars, so her worry that it was broken was a perfectly fair one to raise.
options.why: Comments on what the equipment costs instead of connecting the haze to the lighting.

options.text: I explained to her that the Andromeda galaxy, our nearest large neighbor, is roughly two and a half million light-years from Earth.
options.why: Adds a fact about astronomy but does not explain how the anecdote supports the claim about the lights.

options.text: She was easily the most curious child who has visited our club at any point in the last decade.
options.why: Praises the girl with no support and has no link to the argument about lighting.

options.text: This proves that every city and town in the state would save exactly 18 percent right away by switching to shielded fixtures.
options.why: Overgeneralizes one town's result instead of explaining it.

options.text: Because shielded fixtures stop sending light into the sky, a town pays only for light that actually reaches its streets.
options.why: Uses the wasted light from sentence 9 to explain why shielding reduced Fenwick Ridge's bill.

options.text: Fenwick Ridge is also known for its fall apple festival, which draws visitors from all across the region.
options.why: An irrelevant detail about the town that explains nothing about the evidence.

options.text: Fenwick Ridge, like Larkhaven, is full of residents who care deeply about their community and its long-term future.
options.why: Claims the towns are alike but does not connect the savings to shielding or wasted light.

options.text: Shielded fixtures, which aim light downward toward the street, cost about the same as the city's current globes and last just as long.
options.why: Drops the doubled subject and repeated words but keeps both claims.

options.text: Shielded fixtures, which aim light downward toward the street, they cost about the same as the city's globes and last as long.
options.why: Keeps the extra subject pronoun 'they,' which is ungrammatical.

options.text: Shielded fixtures, which aim light down toward the street below, are similar in cost to the globes the city uses now and are also similar in how long they last.
options.why: Grammatically correct but still wordy and repetitive.

options.text: Shielded fixtures, which aim light downward toward the street, cost somewhat more than the city's current globes but last much longer.
options.why: Changes both claims and weakens the writer's point that switching costs nothing extra.

options.text: Its volunteer roster has grown by a third since, and the average age of a new recruit is twenty-nine.
options.why: Sentence 23 is evidence from the Tillery County example supporting the claim; it reports a result rather than stating the argument.

options.text: These are not isolated anecdotes; they are the shape of the thing.
options.why: Sentence 9 endorses Weil's evidence that decline is real, which the writer accepts, but it does not express her distinctive claim about the cause of that decline or the remedy.

options.text: Weil's reporting is the book's great strength.
options.why: Sentence 5 praises one feature of the book; it is a subordinate judgment that the writer goes on to qualify, not the thesis of the review.

options.text: But obsolete is the wrong word for a system that has been quietly loaded with burdens it was never designed to carry.
options.why: Sentence 13 states the writer's core disagreement with Weil and the alternative diagnosis that paragraphs 3 through 6 develop: the system is overburdened, not obsolete.

options.text: announcing that the review will endorse the book's recommendations for county commissioners without reservation and adopt its proposal for paid crews
options.why: Sentence 4 recommends the book, but paragraph 3 rejects Weil's recommendation to hire paid crews and paragraph 6 urges skepticism.

options.text: pairing the writer's firsthand knowledge with the stakes for county officials, setting up a review that tests the book against experience
options.why: Sentences 1 through 3 establish the writer's experience of understaffed calls, and sentence 4 names both the book and the commissioners who must decide; the rest of the essay measures Weil's diagnosis against what the writer knows.

options.text: introducing the fire levy adopted in Tillery County as the standard by which the book will be judged
options.why: The levy does not appear until paragraph 5; paragraph 1 mentions no remedy of any kind.

options.text: outlining a chronological history of the writer's eleven years with the Marrow Creek company that the later paragraphs will continue year by year
options.why: The paragraph gives a single scene and a credential, and no later paragraph narrates the writer's career in sequence.

options.text: Paragraph 4 restates the burden described in paragraph 3 as an analogy and uses it to expose a question the book never asks
options.why: Sentence 18 renders the self-funded equipment burden of sentence 15 as the lifeguard analogy, and sentence 20 uses that absurdity to pose the question Weil fails to ask.

options.text: Paragraph 4 concedes that Weil's diagnosis in paragraph 3 is correct before offering an alternative remedy drawn from the writer's own years of service
options.why: Sentence 20 criticizes Weil for treating the burden as 'a charming folkway'; paragraph 4 sharpens the disagreement rather than conceding, and it offers no remedy from the writer's service.

options.text: Paragraph 4 narrows the discussion from fundraising to the state training requirement introduced in paragraph 3, treating training hours as the chief burden
options.why: Training is mentioned in sentence 14, but paragraph 4 concerns fundraising for equipment, not training hours.

options.text: Paragraph 4 presents evidence that contradicts the concession the writer makes in paragraph 3 about changed work patterns and distant warehouse jobs
options.why: Paragraph 4 offers no evidence about work patterns; the concession in sentence 12 stands unchallenged throughout the essay.

options.text: It introduces a new criticism of the methods Weil used to gather his figures in six counties, faulting his small sample of stations
options.why: The writer never questions Weil's reporting methods or sample; sentence 5 calls the reporting 'the book's great strength.'

options.text: It qualifies the writer's claim by acknowledging that the levy imposed real costs on Tillery County households that many could not afford
options.why: Sentence 22 minimizes the cost as 'roughly the price of a tank of gas,' which strengthens rather than qualifies the writer's case.

options.text: It answers the question posed at the end of paragraph 4 with a counterexample, giving the final verdict a factual basis
options.why: Sentence 20 asks what happens when the county buys the truck; sentences 22 and 23 report Tillery County's levy and roster growth, which sentence 28's claim that the service 'has a remedy' depends on.

options.text: It summarizes the book's strongest reporting so that the reader can weigh its warning fairly before the conclusion, recalling his aging rosters
options.why: Paragraph 5 presents the writer's own evidence from Tillery County, which sentence 21 says is 'more hopeful than Weil allows'; it is not a summary of the book.

options.text: concede that the volunteer model is in fact beyond saving while urging readers to admire its final years
options.why: Sentence 28 explicitly affirms that the service has a remedy, and sentence 29 tells county boards where to find it.

options.text: characterize Weil's conclusion as a premature death notice, reinforcing the contrast between natural decline and preventable neglect
options.why: 'Obituary' frames Weil's diagnosis of obsolescence as declaring a death; sentence 28 then insists the service is 'not dying of old age' but 'being starved,' a condition with a remedy.

options.text: suggest that the book memorializes, by name, volunteers who died answering calls alone in understaffed counties
options.why: The literal sense of 'obituary' is not in play; the book's described content concerns aging rosters and dissolved companies, not deaths in service.

options.text: mock the book's somber tone as melodramatic, undercutting the praise offered in the preceding sentence
options.why: Sentence 26 calls the portraits 'honest and often moving' and the warning 'overdue'; the writer disputes the diagnosis, not the seriousness of the tone.

options.text: suggesting that maintainers are too easily wounded by ordinary criticism to be trusted with the critical infrastructure that institutions depend on
options.why: The passage's sympathy runs toward maintainers and against those who make demands of them; it faults the dependents, not the volunteers.

options.text: demonstrating that hospital networks are more considerate users of volunteer code than the banks or corporations that send most reports
options.why: The single hospital thank-you is used as a rarity, not as a comparison among institutional types; the passage never ranks hospitals against banks or says who sends most reports.

options.text: establishing the technical authority she needs, as a nine-year maintainer, to challenge the findings and methods of Alcock's survey
options.why: She does not challenge the survey; she endorses the diagnosis in paragraph 2. The anecdote concerns recognition and loneliness, not technical credentials.

options.text: prompting them to recognize that they, too, may have treated an individual volunteer as if she were an anonymous department
options.why: The account of demanding reports is followed by a question asking whether any correspondent imagined 'a person, rather than a department' was reading them, and the essay closes by naming 'the several thousand of us who were standing on her work'; the audience of ordinary users is being implicated in the neglect.

options.text: evidence supporting the writer's concession that sponsorship money has in fact rescued some projects
options.why: It directly follows 'I will grant that money has saved projects' and supplies a specific case of a stipend saving a library, before the rebuttal 'But a stipend changes what the work is.'

options.text: evidence supporting the writer's claim that obligations should be paid in hours rather than dollars
options.why: The example shows money working, which is the opposite of the hours-not-dollars claim; it belongs to the conceded point, not the writer's own remedy.

options.text: evidence that the second half of the book is better written than the first
options.why: Although the writer notes Alcock 'tells that story well,' she has just said the second half 'loses its footing' and never compares the prose quality of the two halves.

options.text: a claim that Alcock's survey of four hundred packages underestimates the role of foundations
options.why: The sentence reports a specific case rather than asserting a general position, and it says nothing about the survey's accuracy.

options.text: Paragraph 2 endorses the book's diagnosis of the problem, and paragraph 3 rejects the book's proposed cure
options.why: Paragraph 2 opens 'The book's first half is a diagnosis, and it is a good one,' and paragraph 3 opens by locating the book's failure 'in the second half, where Alcock turns from diagnosis to cure.'

options.text: Paragraph 2 raises a problem, and paragraph 3 presents the writer's own solution to it
options.why: Paragraph 3 examines and rebuts Alcock's solution; the writer's own solution does not appear until paragraph 5.

options.text: Paragraph 2 states the writer's own thesis, and paragraph 3 supplies further evidence supporting that thesis
options.why: Paragraph 2 summarizes Alcock's findings rather than the writer's thesis, and paragraph 3 turns against the book rather than supporting what precedes it.

options.text: Paragraph 2 praises the book's survey, and paragraph 3 shows that the survey's findings were flawed
options.why: The writer never questions the survey; she continues to accept the diagnosis and later says the first half 'will frighten you in the right way.'

options.text: convey the writer's contempt for a critic who has never maintained software himself and so cannot grasp what volunteer maintainers endure
options.why: The sentence credits Alcock with unmatched understanding; its tone is puzzled and respectful, and the passage never says Alcock lacks maintenance experience or fails to grasp maintainers' situation.

options.text: return the personal testimony of paragraph 4 to the evaluation of the book by tying the lack of recognition to the inadequacy of sponsorship
options.why: After the digression into her own bug reports, the sentence names Alcock again and uses 'this loneliness' to connect the anecdote's point about being unseen to the critique that money cannot address it, preparing the alternative cure in paragraph 5.

options.text: soften the review's criticism by conceding that Alcock's empathy outweighs the weakness of his remedy, so that the second half of the book seems largely redeemed
options.why: The praise of Alcock's understanding is real, but the sentence uses it to sharpen, not soften, the objection: his insight makes the remedy 'puzzling,' and the second half is never redeemed.

options.text: introduce the writer's own proposal that the institutions depending on these libraries should contribute engineers' hours instead of corporate sponsorship money
options.why: The proposal is introduced in the next paragraph with 'The better cure is already visible'; this sentence only diagnoses the mismatch in Alcock's thinking.

options.text: expressing open anger at the hospital network that waited so long, nearly nine years, to finally thank her
options.why: The hospital is the one correspondent who did thank her; the passage directs no anger at it and gives no timing for its message, and the restraint of a single word is the opposite of open anger.

options.text: emphasizing that only one institution, a hospital network in a distant city, was actually using the writer's library
options.why: The 'one' counts thank-you messages, not users; the previous sentence establishes thousands of correspondents, and paragraph 1 refers to companies she could not name.

options.text: isolating the number with wry understatement so that the rarity of gratitude registers more sharply than any complaint could
options.why: The word follows a long sentence cataloguing four thousand demanding reports; its brevity sets the single thank-you apart, and the flat restatement without commentary is understated rather than indignant.

options.text: establishing the writer's credibility by showing she kept precise, dated records of every report she received over nine years
options.why: The passage says 'roughly four thousand,' signalling approximation; the short sentence is about scarcity of thanks, not record-keeping.

options.text: reassuring parents that children are instinctively more disciplined than adults whenever a new device enters the household, and so need no rules at all.
options.why: The passage never generalizes about children's discipline or says they need no rules; it records only that one grandfather was distracted, and later ledgers name 'Dad included' without ranking the generations.

options.text: inviting adult readers to see themselves as possible subjects of the rule, unsettling the pledge's assumption that only children need protecting.
options.why: The audience consists of adults who received a card framed around children; the detail, reinforced by 'All of us' and 'to keep herself and her husband inside as much as anyone,' turns the rule toward the adults reading the essay.

options.text: establishing the grandmother as a careful keeper of household records whose ledger entries the reader can trust as evidence.
options.why: The ledger's precision does build credibility, but that is the work of the price and the dated entries, not of the detail about who was 'the trouble,' which speaks to the audience's assumptions about blame.

options.text: confirming the library's premise that the supper table must be reclaimed on behalf of the young from the adults who neglect it.
options.why: The writer explicitly resists the card's wording and later tells readers to cross out 'Give your children back the table'; the rule is for 'all of us,' not a reclamation on children's behalf.

options.text: narrowing what the shared hour is claimed to have produced from conversation to mere presence, which the writer then argues was itself worth keeping.
options.why: The paragraph shifts the claim from 'produced conversation' to 'produced attendance,' then rebuts with 'attendance, it turns out, is not nothing' and the mother's detailed memory of the sullen suppers.

options.text: admitting that the household rule failed in practice and therefore suggesting that modern families should enforce it less rigidly, perhaps on weekends only.
options.why: The writer does not treat the rule as a failure or call for loosening it; she goes on to sign the card and urge readers to keep the hour 'every night.'

options.text: introducing nostalgia as the chief reason readers should sign the pledge, since remembered suppers, however idealized, matter more than the real ones did.
options.why: Nostalgia is named as a temptation the evidence corrects ('Nostalgia would have me believe'), not as a motive the writer endorses for signing.

options.text: setting aside the documentary record in favor of the writer's own childhood memories, which she presents as more reliable than ledgers or letters.
options.why: The writer relies on the ledgers and letters throughout the concession and cites her mother's memory as additional support, not her own memories as a replacement for the record.

options.text: It defines two key terms in order to clarify the library's wording, which the writer finds ambiguous rather than mistaken and hopes the library will reword.
options.why: The definitions serve the whole argument about rituals, and the writer finds the wording mistaken, not ambiguous, as her instruction to readers to cross it out shows.

options.text: It provides the conceptual distinction that reinterprets the family examples in paragraphs 2 and 3 and sets up the closing instruction about the pledge card.
options.why: The curfew-ritual definition and the whistle-versus-warrant analogy explain why 'All of us' and 'Dad included' mattered, and they ground the final advice to cross out the card's line about children.

options.text: It shifts the evidence from family history to the economic life of the town, broadening the base of support for the writer's argument.
options.why: The mill whistle appears as an analogy for how the rule should feel, not as new evidence about the town's economy; the paragraph's work is conceptual, not evidentiary.

options.text: It anticipates and refutes the objection about sullen, silent suppers that the writer raises in the paragraph that follows, defusing it before it appears.
options.why: Paragraph 4 says nothing about the quality of the suppers; the concession is raised and answered within paragraph 5 itself.

options.text: a chain of causes and effects, which shows that each new device forced the household to make the previous rule stricter than before.
options.why: The paragraph presents the rules as the same response each time, not as an escalating sequence in which one device caused a stricter rule for the next.

options.text: a problem-and-solution structure, which proposes unplugging devices as the remedy for the family quarrels each machine provoked at the supper table in turn.
options.why: No quarrels are described in paragraph 3, and the writer stresses that the machines were not removed but scheduled ('it told the stranger when to call').

options.text: a contrast between generations, which exposes the grandmother's leniency toward the radio against the mother's far greater severity toward the television nearly thirty years later.
options.why: Both women wrote nearly identical rules ('All of us'; 'no exceptions, Dad included'); the paragraph stresses continuity, not a difference in strictness.

options.text: a chronological series of parallel examples, which establishes that the household's response to each new device was a repeated pattern rather than a single quirk.
options.why: The paragraph lists 1954 and 1967 in parallel sentences after announcing 'The pattern repeated itself,' and concludes with 'each time the household did the same thing.'

options.text: a settled conclusion that distills the three-generation narrative into one principle, their brevity lending the writer's stance an air of certainty.
options.why: After long sentences of instruction and narrative, the clipped pair reduces the radio, telephone, television and phone to 'the machine' and the recurring rule to 'the fence,' and the terse rhythm reads as assured finality.

options.text: a new counterargument about whether a rule from 1938 can still apply to devices that fit in a pocket.
options.why: The sentences answer, rather than raise, the question of applicability; the writer has already extended the rule to phones ('phone in the drawer') in the preceding sentence.

options.text: a resigned acknowledgment that new technology will keep arriving no matter what households decide to do about it.
options.why: The sentences are not resigned; the stress falls on the unchanged fence, which the writer treats as a dependable and chosen response, not on technology's inevitability.

options.text: a late reservation that the household rule, described as a fence, may now confine the family more than it protects them.
options.why: The word 'fence' has been established since paragraph 2 as a shared boundary built 'to keep herself and her husband inside'; nothing in the ending reverses that positive sense.

options.text: A request from apprentices that the association deliver its training through video so that they can learn at their own pace
options.why: The proposal comes from the board, not the apprentices, and the writer presents apprentices as beneficiaries of the program rather than as advocates for its replacement.

options.text: A shortage of retired members willing to volunteer their time, which has left most apprentices without an assigned mentor for the coming year
options.why: The passage never mentions a shortage of volunteers; the retired members are described as present, if 'set in their ways.'

options.text: A disagreement between the writer and her former mentor about whether new diagnostic tools belong in the hands of first-year apprentices
options.why: Augie and the thermal camera appear as illustrations within the argument; no dispute with Augie about tools is described, and the occasion is the board memo.

options.text: A proposal under consideration by the writer's association to replace a mentorship program with recorded training materials ahead of a scheduled vote
options.why: Paragraph 1 identifies the board memo proposing to end the ride-along program in favor of training videos and the writer's intent to argue against it 'before the vote next month.'

options.text: Paragraph 3 turns to a different subject, the value of videos for code updates, leaving paragraph 2 as personal background
options.why: The remark that a video carries written-down knowledge is a brief concession within the distinction, not a new subject; the paragraph's weight falls on the knowledge that lives only in a person.

options.text: Paragraph 3 qualifies paragraph 2 by conceding that the writer's experience with one mentor may not represent the program as a whole
options.why: Paragraph 3 contains no such concession; it treats the Augie episode as the model of how a habit 'is transferred' rather than as a possibly unrepresentative case.

options.text: Paragraph 3 draws a general distinction between two kinds of knowledge out of the specific lesson narrated in paragraph 2
options.why: The basement scene (the hum, the hand on the pipe) becomes in paragraph 3 the example of a 'habit of noticing' that 'no camera records,' and the paragraph ends by returning to 'the way Augie transferred it.'

options.text: Paragraph 3 refutes the harsh method of instruction described in paragraph 2 by proposing a gentler way to teach attentiveness
options.why: Far from refuting Augie's method, paragraph 3 endorses it as the only way a habit is transferred, 'by standing next to someone long enough.'

options.text: present the second clause as a tentative afterthought that the writer adds in case the first clause seems too strong
options.why: The second clause is the stronger and more definite of the two, stating what has actually happened; nothing in its wording is tentative.

options.text: balance the board's intended result against the actual result in two matched clauses, so the correction lands as a verdict
options.why: The semicolon joins two parallel 'you have' clauses without a conjunction, setting 'not made the program efficient' directly against 'removed the thing it was for' and giving the second clause the force of a judgment.

options.text: introduce a list of the program's purposes that the board's memo has overlooked in its calculation of cost
options.why: No list follows the semicolon; it is a single clause, and the uncounted benefits appear in paragraph 6, not here.

options.text: mark a pause that softens the writer's criticism of the board by separating it from the sharper claim that follows
options.why: The tight pairing of clauses intensifies rather than softens; the writer has just insisted the expense is 'the whole point' and uses the semicolon to deliver the blunt consequence.

options.text: Anyone who still trusts a phone over a printed book has simply not been paying attention to their own garden.
options.why: Insults the very audience she hopes to persuade.

options.text: Libraries hold a quiet charm, with the smell of old paper and the hush of readers turning pages on a rainy afternoon.
options.why: Nostalgic description offers no reason that matters to gardeners and states no position.

options.text: Libraries remain essential institutions for cultivating information literacy, civic engagement, and lifelong learning in a democratic, digitally saturated, and rapidly changing society.
options.why: Abstract, academic language ignores the gardeners' practical needs and the flyer's casual register.

options.text: For gardeners who care about what actually grows in this clay, the library offers local know-how and free seeds that a phone cannot.
options.why: Speaks to the gardeners' practical concern (results in local soil) and previews the library's concrete benefits.

options.text: The Pell Street branch holds more than eleven thousand books, including two full shelves on vegetables, herbs, and fruit trees, plus a rack of glossy national gardening magazines.
options.why: Describes the collection's size but not that local knowledge solved a problem.

options.text: Many online articles about blossom-end rot recommend adding calcium, though they often disagree about the right amount to use and how often to apply it.
options.why: Shifts focus to online advice instead of showing what the library's knowledge accomplished.

options.text: The old notes warned that our clay stays soggy, so I watered less and more evenly, and my July tomatoes came in without a single rotten spot.
options.why: Shows the local, clay-specific advice producing a concrete result, directly supporting sentence 6.

options.text: Mr. Dowd has worked at the branch for nearly twenty years, is known for remembering every regular patron's name, and runs the Thursday story hour for children.
options.why: Builds credibility for the librarian but offers no evidence about the advice's results.

options.text: Search engines are fine for quick questions, and they are usually the best source for advice about our clay.
options.why: Concedes so much that it contradicts the writer's argument about local knowledge.

options.text: Search engines are fine for quick questions, but they cannot tell you how a seed behaves in Hollins Lane clay.
options.why: Concedes a legitimate use and then restates the library's local advantage.

options.text: Search engines, which were invented only a few decades ago, have changed how nearly every person finds recipes, directions, and news.
options.why: Offers a general observation rather than qualifying the claim about gardeners.

options.text: Search engines are almost always useless for gardeners and should rarely, if ever, be trusted by anyone working a plot.
options.why: Softens the wording slightly but still grants search engines no reasonable use.

options.text: Her reference to the audience's years of training and to the drawings, models and cost estimates they will soon control
options.why: Paragraph 3 says 'You have spent years learning to call things by their proper names,' and paragraph 5 says 'You will be the ones in the room' with 'the drawings, the models, the cost estimates,' assuming an audience of newly trained planners about to hold decision-making authority.

options.text: Her careful distinction between forest old growth and street old growth, which presumes an audience of forestry scientists
options.why: The definition in paragraph 2 is offered because the term 'does not fit perfectly' on a street, clarifying for planners, not addressing forestry specialists.

options.text: Her criticism of the council's budgeting, which presumes the listeners are the elected officials who cast last Tuesday's vote on Calder
options.why: The council is discussed in the third person throughout; the audience is told they will be in the room for 'the next Calder Avenue,' not that they cast last Tuesday's vote.

options.text: Her description of the raccoon hollow and the lightning scar, which presumes an audience of residents attached to the avenue
options.why: The opening details build the speaker's own relationship to the trees; the passage addresses 'Graduates' and 'planners,' not the general public of Harrow Fen.

options.text: weaken her central claim by admitting that the council's traffic rationale might sometimes be sufficient
options.why: She concedes only that dangerous trees must be removed; she immediately rejects the traffic rationale as 'a fraction of a minute,' never granting it could suffice.

options.text: reveal that her attachment to the trees has compromised her ability to judge the council's proposal fairly
options.why: Her sleepless night shows feeling, but the concession demonstrates the opposite: she acts on evidence even against her feelings, which strengthens rather than compromises her judgment.

options.text: establish that her objection is not sentimental and narrow her claim to removals that lack adequate justification
options.why: By citing her own signed removal order for the rotted oak and calling a dangerous tree 'a liability with leaves,' she proves she accepts justified removals, then pivots with 'But the Calder sycamores are not dangerous' to confine her argument to unjustified cases.

options.text: propose that all future removal orders be reviewed by an independent board of certified arborists before final approval
