options.why: No independent board is mentioned; the standard she later proposes is that removals be justified 'reluctantly, publicly, and with the arithmetic on the table.'

options.text: classifying the sycamores by their age and condition to identify which of the sixty-one trees most deserve protection from the widening
options.why: The paragraph treats the canopy as a whole and never sorts individual trees by age or condition.

options.text: narrating the stages of her career to show how her understanding of trees matured over several decades of municipal work
options.why: Career narration appears in paragraphs 1 and 4; paragraph 3 contains no personal chronology.

options.text: pairing each tree benefit with a piece of built infrastructure to expose an inconsistency in how the town treats the two
options.why: The paragraph sets a storm sewer beside a sycamore's rainfall capture, a transformer beside the canopy's cooling, and a bridge beside the trees, culminating in the contrast between forty years of culvert maintenance and an afternoon vote to erase the canopy.

options.text: explaining step by step the process by which a mature canopy intercepts rainfall before it reaches the sewer
options.why: Rainfall interception is stated in a single clause with a figure; no process is traced, and the paragraph moves on to cooling and bridges.

options.text: present the council's two decisions as equally reasonable responses to the different lifespans of culverts and trees, each handled according to its expected years of service
options.why: The opening 'Yet' and the contrast between 'forty years' and 'a hundred and forty years... in an afternoon' frame the decisions as inconsistent, not equally reasonable.

options.text: signal through the closing clause that the speaker accepts the balance sheet as the proper measure of a tree's value to the town
options.why: The final clause explains the council's error; the speaker's whole paragraph argues that the balance sheet omits a real asset, so she rejects it as the measure.

options.text: mirror the slow growth of the canopy through a sentence whose length forces the listener to wait as the trees have waited
options.why: Nothing in the sentence links its length to tree growth; the length results from the subordinate clauses that hold the contrast and its cause together.

options.text: bind the council's two contradictory actions to a single subject and delay the explanation to a final clause that exposes an accounting blind spot
options.why: The relative clause 'that budgets forty years of maintenance for a culvert' and the main verb 'will vote to erase' share one subject, 'the same council,' making the contradiction inescapable; the sentence withholds 'because a tree... does not appear on the balance sheet' until the end, so the cause lands as a revelation.

options.text: A mainland colleague has argued that a skilled teacher can turn any ordinary space, even a parking lot, into a laboratory.
options.why: The colleague's objection in paragraph 4 is one voice the writer answers, but the occasion that prompts the column is the board's spring-meeting question and the coming autumn vote, not the colleague's remark.

options.text: The Trust's board has questioned whether a costly offshore program is justified when similar lessons might be taught on shore.
options.why: Paragraph 2 states directly that the board 'asked a fair question' about whether the program is 'really worth running' given the ferry, tide window and alternative of a heated mainland room, and the final paragraph asks the board to keep funding it.

options.text: Enrollment in the Keeper's School has fallen sharply this year because many students become seasick on the ferry crossing to the dock.
options.why: The passage mentions seasickness as an inconvenience but gives no indication that enrollment has dropped; it reports fourteen classes and 312 visiting students without any decline.

options.text: The lighthouse was decommissioned decades ago, and the Trust must now decide whether to restore its working lamp for passing ships.
options.why: The 1994 decommissioning appears only in the closing sentences as a point of ironic contrast; nothing in the passage concerns restoring the light, and the decision at issue is about the ferry and the program.

options.text: signal the writer's lingering uncertainty about whether the expense of the ferry can really be defended before the skeptical members of the board
options.why: The surrounding sentences are confident and conclusive ('But the parking lot does not flood on schedule'), and the final paragraph asks the board outright to keep the ferry running; nothing marks hesitation.

options.text: concede that the program's lessons could be delivered just as well in a heated mainland classroom by any skilled teacher, without the ferry
options.why: This reverses the writer's position; paragraph 2 insists 'the same lessons cannot be taught there,' and the sentence that follows the concession explains why a parking lot cannot substitute for the lighthouse.

options.text: establish the colleague as an authority whose judgment the writer ultimately adopts in place of her own view of the program's worth
options.why: The writer calls the colleague 'thoughtful' but rejects her conclusion in the very next sentence; the concession is strategic, not a deferral to authority.

options.text: grant part of the colleague's premise so the argument can turn from the quality of the teacher to the properties of the place
options.why: The concession accepts the colleague's point about teachers and is immediately followed by 'But the parking lot does not...' which shifts the issue to what only the site provides, culminating in the distinction between questions and consequences.

options.text: conceding the program's practical costs while keeping the claim focused on what the site alone can teach
options.why: The writer lists cost, cancellations and seasickness candidly, then narrows the dispute to teaching value: 'The teacher supplies the questions; the lighthouse supplies the consequences.' Her claim was never about convenience, so the admission limits without undermining it.

options.text: restricting the claim so that it applies only to students who are not made ill by the ferry crossing
options.why: Seasickness is named as one inconvenience among several; the writer never limits who benefits, and the postcard evidence in paragraph 5 treats all 312 visitors as the relevant group.

options.text: acknowledging that the board's financial objections outweigh the educational benefits the students gain from the visits
options.why: The writer admits cost but concludes that the board should keep the ferry running; she never grants that expense outweighs benefit.

options.text: handing the board specific reasons for cancellation that the remainder of the column fails to answer
options.why: The concession is answered immediately by the rebuttal in the same paragraph and by the evidence of lasting impact in paragraph 5; it is the setup for the rebuttal, not an unanswered weakness.

options.text: Paragraph 3 praises the lighthouse's tasks; paragraph 4 contradicts that praise by admitting the tasks are too difficult for students.
options.why: Paragraph 4 concedes logistical inconvenience for the Trust and discomfort on the ferry, not that the tasks are too hard, and it ends by reaffirming the value of the site rather than contradicting paragraph 3.

options.text: Paragraph 3 presents the site's demands as lessons; paragraph 4 anticipates the objection that those demands are merely costs and answers it.
options.why: Paragraph 3 argues that reading tides, climbing and sighting the shoal are lessons in observation; paragraph 4 admits the inconvenience and expense those demands create, voices the colleague's objection, and rebuts it by insisting the place supplies consequences a parking lot cannot.

options.text: Paragraph 3 states the thesis in general terms; paragraph 4 supplies the statistical evidence that proves the thesis to the board.
options.why: The thesis is stated in paragraph 2, and the figures in paragraph 4 (ferry cost, cancelled classes) are concessions about expense, not proof of the thesis; the supporting data appear in paragraph 5.

options.text: Paragraph 3 describes the keepers' historical logbooks; paragraph 4 turns to an unrelated discussion of the Trust's finances and ferry schedule.
options.why: The logbooks are one example in paragraph 3, not its subject, and paragraph 4's cost figures and cancellations are tied directly to the colleague's objection and the rebuttal, so they are not unrelated.

options.text: Perhaps the council could keep half of the block quiet and give the other half to enrichment sessions.
options.why: Proposes a compromise that partly accepts the change the writer opposes.

options.text: That water stain in Room 114 may never look the same to me, since it gave me my best story idea.
options.why: Revisits one anecdote rather than closing the argument or addressing the vote.

options.text: People throughout history have complained about boredom, and students everywhere will probably keep complaining about it for many centuries to come.
options.why: Drifts to boredom in general and never mentions the vote or makes a request.

options.text: When the council votes next month, I hope its members will leave those twenty-five empty minutes exactly as they are.
options.why: Names the vote from sentence 3 and asks the council to keep the block unchanged, fitting the editorial's purpose.

options.text: Every single student at Marlow Ridge agrees with me, so council members have no choice but to vote the proposal down.
options.why: Makes a sweeping claim the draft never supports and pressures rather than persuades.

options.text: Council members surely know best, so I will happily trust whatever new schedule they decide on for our Tuesday afternoons this year.
options.why: Respectful but abandons the writer's position.

options.text: Clearly the council has never had an original thought, so it is no surprise they want to schedule ours for us.
options.why: Insults the very readers the writer must persuade.

options.text: I ask council members to weigh what students would lose before trading the week's only unscheduled stretch for one more schedule.
options.why: Respectful toward the council, keeps the writer's opposition, and gives them a reason to reconsider.

options.text: The council should keep the quiet block, because enrichment sessions would cost the school money and require extra training for every teacher.
options.why: Previews cost and staffing points the editorial never develops.

options.text: The council should keep the quiet block, because its boredom has sparked real student work and even its idle moments have value.
options.why: States a debatable position and previews paragraph 2 (student work) and paragraph 3 (answering critics about idleness).

options.text: The council should keep the quiet block, because I personally like having a relaxing break in the middle of each long Tuesday.
options.why: Takes a position but rests on preference and does not preview the student examples or rebuttal.

options.text: The quiet block is a twenty-five-minute period that takes place every Tuesday right after lunch in the classrooms of Marlow Ridge High.
options.why: States a fact, not an arguable claim, and previews nothing.

options.text: A runner who skips every practice in the weeks before a big race is likely to finish far behind the runners who trained steadily.
options.why: Suggests inactivity leads to failure, the opposite of the writer's point.

options.text: A farmer who leaves a field unplanted for a season is not wasting it; she is letting the soil recover for the next harvest.
options.why: Fallow-field comparison shows apparent idleness as preparation for later productivity.

options.text: The word boredom comes from an older English term, and its meaning has shifted a great deal over the centuries since it first appeared in print.
options.why: Offers word history, not a comparison, and does not advance the rebuttal.

options.text: A student who sleeps through a math lecture is being rude to a teacher who spent hours the night before preparing the day's lesson.
options.why: Treats sleeping as a failure, supporting the critics rather than the writer.

options.text: Birchfield residents chose to live far from town, after all, and they should simply accept the long drive that comes with that choice.
options.why: Makes an unfair assumption about commuters and offers them nothing, so it undercuts the concession.

options.text: Retiming the light and adding a turn lane at Mill Road could win back most of those ten minutes without removing a single bench.
options.why: Takes the commuters' concern seriously and offers a concrete fix that keeps the sidewalks.

options.text: Traffic has grown steadily across the whole county as new housing keeps going up on the edges of town, from Birchfield to the river flats.
options.why: Shifts to county-wide trends and does not address what commuters need.

options.text: Commuters could simply leave home ten minutes earlier each morning, as the rest of us managed to do long before Birchfield was ever built.
options.why: Brushes off and talks down to the very readers the writer wants to win over.

options.text: A bench turns someone passing through into someone who lingers, and people who linger are the ones who wander inside to buy.
options.why: Spells out the cause and effect that links the benches and sales to the claim about slowness.

options.text: A rise of nearly a third is a large increase for any small business, especially in a town of this size.
options.why: Points out how big the number is but never connects it to slow, lingering foot traffic.

options.text: Benches are inexpensive, so the town could easily afford to install more of them on Linden Row and other streets next year.
options.why: Moves to cost and other streets, which is off the paragraph's claim.

options.text: Rosa has run the hardware store on Quarry Street ever since her father retired from it in 2004 and moved to the coast.
options.why: Gives background about the owner and does not explain the evidence.

options.text: I would ask the engineers behind this plan to walk Quarry Street on a weekday morning before the vote.
options.why: Makes a direct, polite request that keeps the point without insulting anyone.

options.text: Perhaps, if it isn't too much trouble, someone might glance at the street at some point, whenever it happens to be convenient.
options.why: So timid and vague that the firmness the writer wants is lost.

options.text: Engineers widen streets because traffic data from every town show that wider lanes always reduce congestion and never slow anyone down.
options.why: Makes an absolute claim with no support, and it works against the writer's own argument.

options.text: Whoever dreamed up this plan should be far too embarrassed to show their face at the March 14 meeting.
options.why: Even more insulting than the original and would push decision-makers away.

content.text:
I rewrote six distractors and left the other three as they were. No stem, option order or keyed answer was changed.

- **Question 1:** I lengthened all three wrong options. Option 1 is now 25 words against the key's 22, so it's the one distractor longer than the key. In option 2, the added clause notes that the brown departed from the state style guide. That's true in the passage, but the option still claims a concession that never happens, so it stays wrong.
- **Question 2:** I lengthened all three wrong options to 23–25 words. The key is 25.
- **Question 3:** I added two words to option 1, bringing it to 21. Options 2 and 3 were already 21 words, so I left them alone.

Every distractor keeps its original flaw type. Its "why" changed only where the claim changed. No option goes over 25 words.

options.text: evidence that a single design choice shaped the board's decision, supporting the claim that maps make a case rather than merely report
options.why: The members' testimony links the color choice directly to the outcome, which is exactly what the thesis in paragraph 1 and the definition in paragraph 2 assert about selection and emphasis.

options.text: evidence that Quist knowingly misled the board by exaggerating the danger of flooding along the terrace, using a color chosen to frighten rather than inform
options.why: The passage presents the brown shading and the printed flood crest as accurate data made emphatic, and paragraph 4 explicitly denies that emphasis equals deception.

options.text: a concession that the developers' attorney was right to call the map inflammatory, since its brown departed from the state style guide
options.why: Quist's reply in the preceding sentence turns the charge around rather than conceding it, and the vote detail is offered as proof of effect, not as an admission.

options.text: a claim that the board reached the correct decision in rejecting construction on the river's lower terrace, proving the developers' plans unsafe
options.why: The writer never judges whether the vote was right or the plans unsafe; the sentence reports what members remembered, not whether the project deserved rejection.

options.text: suggest that the floodplain map was only partly accurate because its brown shading overstated the actual danger posed by the river's past floods
options.why: 'Half' refers to half of the critics' charge, not to the map's accuracy; the passage never questions the data, only the color used to present it.

options.text: weaken the writer's own standing by confessing that personal loyalty to a former teacher has biased this account of her career and her disputes
options.why: The concession is about Quist's stance, not the writer's loyalty; it strengthens the writer's credibility by showing fairness to critics before the rebuttal.

options.text: acknowledge that the critics were correct in judging Quist unqualified to serve as a surveyor for the county, whatever her skill with a drafting pen
options.why: The half granted concerns only her wish to stop the project; the writer concedes nothing about her qualifications and the passage records forty-three years of county work.

options.text: accept that Quist held a position on the project while rejecting the premise that any map can lack an advocate, shifting the issue to openness
options.why: The next sentences grant that she wanted the project stopped, then deny that a map without an advocate exists, and the paragraph ends by relocating her distinction to the fact that she signed the argument.

options.text: Paragraph 3 supplies an example that invites an objection, and paragraph 4 states that objection and answers it to sharpen the claim
options.why: The floodplain story prompts the critics' charge of advocacy, which paragraph 4 raises, half concedes, and rebuts, arriving at the refined claim that she signed the argument.

options.text: Paragraph 3 praises Quist's boldness, and paragraph 4 retracts that praise by admitting her brown map distorted the county's flood data
options.why: Paragraph 4 concedes only that she had a position; it insists the data were sound and that the supposedly neutral map was equally advocated.

options.text: Paragraph 3 describes a local dispute, and paragraph 4 broadens it into a judgment about the ethics of all public officials
options.why: Paragraph 4 stays within cartography, discussing whether any map lacks an advocate; it makes no claim about public officials generally.

options.text: Paragraph 3 offers one example of Quist's persuasive maps, and paragraph 4 adds a second example drawn from a different commission
options.why: Paragraph 4 contains no new commission; it returns to the same pale blue floodplain to argue about advocacy.

options.text: Cutler's Marsh has quite a history, and it will be interesting to watch what the council finally decides.
options.why: Observes rather than urging any action.

options.text: Seriously, anyone who votes against the marsh plan is clueless and should just stay home this spring.
options.why: Insulting and slangy, unfit for a respectful editorial.

options.text: Our biology teachers already have lab equipment, so outdoor water testing would cost the school nothing.
options.why: Adds a new unsupported claim rather than concluding with a call to action.

options.text: Before the spring vote, ask your parents to write the council and support bringing Cutler's Marsh back.
options.why: Uses an appropriate tone and gives readers a concrete action tied to the vote.

options.text: Restoring the marsh would likely reduce the flooding that Brambleton suffers after heavy rains.
options.why: Softens the absolute claim to one the sponge explanation and flood example can support.

options.text: Restoring the marsh would probably have no real effect on flooding along Finch Lane at all.
options.why: Contradicts the writer's argument and evidence.

options.text: Restoring the marsh would certainly stop all flooding in Brambleton and the rest of Larkfield.
options.why: Makes the claim even more absolute and widens its scope.

options.text: Restoring the marsh might perhaps help with water in a few places now and then.
options.why: Qualifies the claim but hedges so heavily that it no longer makes a useful point.

options.text: Similarly,
options.why: Signals likeness, but the finding opposes the worry.

options.text: Consequently,
options.why: Implies the worry caused the finding.

options.text: However,
options.why: Signals contrast between the worry and the evidence that answers it.

options.text: For instance,
options.why: Presents the finding as an example of the worry rather than a rebuttal.

options.text: Some residents are freaking out big time about a bunch of mosquitoes.
options.why: Keeps slang that dismisses the concern.

options.text: Some paranoid residents irrationally panic over the idea of mosquitoes.
options.why: Insults residents rather than presenting them respectfully.

options.text: Some residents have mosquitoes, which they worry about in their water.
options.why: Unclear, awkward wording that changes the meaning.

options.text: Some residents are understandably worried that standing water will bring mosquitoes.
options.why: Respectful, measured wording that sets up the rebuttal fairly.
